video.title: He Built a Simple App and Sold It for $200 Million

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Dan Porter, former teacher and CEO of OMGPOP, who designed Draw Something, a friends-only drawing game that hit #1 in 60 countries with 25M daily players and sold to Zynga for $200M. He explains the key ingredients (simplicity, streaks, friends-only play, live drawing playback) and how a bug fix made it take off. He later led digital at WME and founded Overtime (110M followers, own leagues) and launched 67 Water from a meme. Key takeaway: building is research, small tweaks matter, and hits need all ingredients together.

ideas.name: Draw Something: simple friends-only social mobile game
ideas.one_liner: A drawing-and-guessing mobile game played only with friends, with streaks instead of winners and live playback of drawings; hit #1 and sold to Zynga for $200M.

ideas.customer: Mobile phone users of all ages, including 80-year-olds
ideas.problem: Open-lobby drawing games were toxic; games were competitive and complex
ideas.offer: Friend-based Pictionary-style game with streaks, live drawing playback, touch-native mechanics

tactics.name: Fix toxicity by restricting the audience
steps: Identify why an open version fails (strangers being rude)
Limit play to friends instead of moderating everyone
Gain built-in virality from contact invites

quote.text: you couldn't solve changing people's bad behavior on the internet
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Check analytics for your real customer
steps: Discover real audience (14-year-old girls in California, not the team)
Rename company if users misspell it

quote.text: I realized that the customers were actually almost entirely 14-year-old girls in California
quote.speaker: Dan Porter

tactics.name: Hiring question for designers
steps: Ask 'what is your favourite game?' then 'why is it great?'
Hire the 1 in 5 who describe a specific mechanic in depth

tactics.name: Paid filmer network instead of UGC
steps: Pay people $20 per game to film

tactics.name: Street-level customer development
steps: Send interns to bodegas/gas stations to talk to owners and kids
Feed findings into product (e.g. add a flavour)
Launch in an overlooked market (Kentucky) not LA/NY

warnings.warning: Platform risk cuts both ways: a giant platform game (FarmVille) made his company small overnight.

quote.text: All of a sudden we were big and then we were small
quote.speaker: Dan Porter

warnings.warning: A technical bug nearly killed the hit; it bombed until developers noticed people trying to play.

quote.text: If they don't say that, the app doesn't blow up and the company goes out of business
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

warnings.warning: Building for 'people like us' rather than real users.
Young people don't go to websites.

quote.text: Like have you ever seen a young person open a browser on their phone?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

warnings.warning: Owning many businesses at once makes it hard to make any great.

lessons.lesson: Hits need all key ingredients together (simplicity, streaks, friends-only, live playback); remove one and it fails.

quote.text: You take one of those four key ingredients away, then it's a nothing burger
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Building is the research; a premise is just an excuse to start.

quote.text: the building of the thing is the best research you can do
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Small tweaks can be the difference between failure and $200M; keep testing.
Outsiders can win because they don't know the 'right' way (forgot to add XP).
Great products must feel amazing in use.
Hire people who think deeply about why things work.
Passion often follows being good at something.
Launch where competition for attention is lower (Kentucky, not LA/NY).
Cultural signals (wired headphones, recurring story themes) inform product decisions.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand founder with headline figures, little unit economics; mostly lessons.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Sponsor read for Beehiiv; TKOwners promo.
